title: Six ways to read a sequence
goal: List the six reading frames of a DNA sequence and find which ones have no stop codon.
answer_format: the frame labels with no stop codon, separated by commas (for example +2, -1)
background:
A stretch of DNA doesn't say where its codons begin. Starting at base 1, 2 or 3
gives three different ways to cut it into codons, called reading frames. The other
strand gives three more, so every piece of DNA has six reading frames.

We label them +1, +2 and +3 for the given strand, starting at its base 1, 2 or 3,
and -1, -2 and -3 for the reverse complement, starting at its base 1, 2 or 3.
Translate each frame for as many complete codons as fit.

In random DNA, about 3 of every 64 codons are stops, so long stretches without a
stop are unusual. A frame without stops is a hint that a protein-coding gene might
be there.
prompt:
For the short read in your data file, translate all six frames. Which frames contain
no stop codon at all?

hints.text: Start with the three frames on the given strand. What changes between frame +1 and frame +2?
Where do the other three frames come from? You wrote the function you need in an earlier problem.
For each frame, take the sequence from base 1, 2 or 3 (substring(s, k)), translate the complete codons, and check grepl('*', protein, fixed = TRUE). Do this for the reverse complement too.
